newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece says no face-to-face meeting with Turks.
newsitem.headline: Greece says no face-to-face meeting with Turks.

text.p: Greece said on Wednesday a group of experts formed to help resolve thorny differences between it and neighbouring Turkey would not actually meet face-to-face.

Greece proposed earlier this month setting up a committee from both countries to discuss procedural issues relating to Greek-Turkish disputes, which have long soured relations between the two NATO members.
"There will not be a joint meeting between the teams of experts," Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told a news conference.
He said the two groups would communicate through the Dutch presidency of the European Union, which has been trying to mediate between the feuding countries.

The prospect of talks with Turkey angered many within Greece's ruling socialist party and 32 deputies signed an open letter to the government last week warning against too close contact with Turkey while contentious issues remained unresolved.

The government has refused to comment on the letter, saying it was an internal party affair, but political analysts said it made clear not all socialists shared technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis's vision of rapprochement with Turkey.
Athens and Ankara have long been at odds over territorial differences in the Aegean Sea, minorities in both countries and the divided island of Cyprus.
European Union member Greece has blocked Turkey's efforts to get closer to the 15-member bloc, citing what it sees as aggression from Ankara and a poor human rights record.

Cyprus, which also wants to join the EU, has been divided since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded and occupied its northern third after a coup attempt in Nicosia engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece.

The EU was delighted to see the first signs of rapprochement last week when Greek Deputy Foreign Minister George Papandreou met his Turkish counterpart Onur Oymen on the fringes of a Malta conference.

It was the first time the two countries had talked since January last year when they almost clashed over two uninhabited islets in the eastern Aegean. Hostilities were averted by a last-minute U.S. intervention.

Ankara has repeatedly called for direct dialogue to resolve differences. Athens has adamantly rejected this, saying it would never negotiate its borders, and wants Turkey to take its territorial claims to the International Court at the Hague.
